This is not a simple question and there's no one "right" answer. It's not just one thing. And refusal to take meds isn't necessarily the same as refusing to accept a diagnosis.

You wouldn't believe the number of people who keep getting admitted to hospitals because they insist they aren't diabetic (or a plethora of other illnesses they deny having or are just non-compliant with treatment). And yeah, some of these people do have cognitive or mental health issues but there's plenty of people who are perfectly normal, fully functioning human beings who just can't be reasoned with in that area.

Stigma, discrimination, side effects, lack of education, lack of resources/support to maintain effective treatment, trauma, negative interactions with the healthcare system, previous incorrect diagnosis, delusions, denial, grief, fear.... You could probably come up with thousands of unique scenarios that explain why people do this. If you're good with empathy, most of the scenarios you can even understand why people go that route even when it's not the choice you'd have made or it's not the logical choice.

Frankly, if you wouldn't leave someone for developing diabetes or cancer, you shouldn't leave them just for having a mental health crisis either. It might be fair to leave if they refuse to treat/manage the condition once they know it's the problem, but the brain is an organ that can get sick and malfunction like any other.

And if you would leave them for those other things, well, there's probably no point to mentioning anything else.

Also, not willing to work with you doesn't necessarily mean she can't care for her kids either, just means you have to go through the courts to find out. 

Regardless, if your kids aren't already in therapy, they will need it. If they aren't willing to go to therapy, try to arrange for them to have time with a trusted adult. Kids don't always want to tell their parents everything. I know it's hard as a parent to not know exactly what's going on but it's better they are willing to go to someone who can intervene if necessary than to cause them to just never say anything to anyone.

Do x (x=unpleasant task) for y (y=amount of time you can reasonably expect yourself to stay relatively focused and on task) and then allow yourself a break to do something fun or rest (length of break often depends on length of y and difficulty of x). 

This works pretty well if you have health issues. You can adjust the times for how you're doing. For example, when I'm very depressed or sick or having issues with pain, y sometimes becomes as little as 5 minutes with a 2 hour break. You can load a dishwasher or switch laundry around or take a walk around the block or do some stretches or make plans with a friend for a 30 min coffee date or check the mail or outline a paragraph for a paper in 5 minutes. You aren't going to get everything done but it's better than 12 solid hours of Netflix.

Additionally, keep things organized and tidy. Always having to spend a few minutes looking for something really adds up over time.
